title: University of Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence 2027: Applications Open for Interdisciplinary AI Doctoral Research
summary: Applications are now open for the University of Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence , an interdisciplinary doctoral programme designed for researchers who want to advance artificial intelligence while keeping human needs, capabilities, ethics, governance and social impact at the centre of technological development. Hosted by the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence (CHIA) within Cambridge’s Institute for Technology and Humanity (ITH) , the programme brings together technical AI research with perspectives from the humanities, social sciences, health, ethics, policy and other human-centred disciplines. Its stated goal is to train a new generation of AI researchers, technologists and leaders capable of developing AI that is human-centred, human-compatible, responsible and socially and globally beneficial. Research areas highlighted by Cambridge include: Fundamental human-level AI Social and interactive AI Cognitive AI Creative AI Health and global AI Responsible AI The programme is particularly distinctive because it does not treat artificial intelligence as exclusively a computer science problem. Students are expected to engage with the technical, ethical, human, applied and industrial dimensions of AI, making the PhD suitable for ambitious interdisciplinary projects that combine computational research with questions about people and society. Applications for Michaelmas 2027 entry opened on 9 September 2026 . The main application and course funding deadline is: 8 December 2026 The course is scheduled to begin on: 1 October 2027 Applicants seeking consideration in the Gates Cambridge U.S. round face an earlier funding deadline of: 14 October 2026. About the Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence The PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence has been created in response to the rapid expansion of AI across research, industry, government, civil society and everyday life. Cambridge s approach recognizes that the future of AI depends on more than increasing computational power or creating more sophisticated algorithms. AI systems interact with people, institutions, cultures and political and economic structures, raising difficult questions about: Human behaviour Trust Responsibility Governance Creativity Cognition Health Social interaction Ethics Safety Global inequality Technology s effects on institutions and society The programme therefore takes a deliberately interdisciplinary and cross-disciplinary approach to technical AI . Students are based at CHIA while also potentially working with researchers and facilities across other parts of the University of Cambridge. Possible arrangements can include: Cross-disciplinary supervision Co-supervision Participation in research seminars Collaboration with other university units Access to relevant facilities across Cambridge The intention is to allow PhD researchers to build projects that are technically serious while also engaging deeply with the human implications of AI. About the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence The programme is based in the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence , or CHIA. CHIA sits within the University of Cambridge s Institute for Technology and Humanity and provides an interdisciplinary environment for researchers examining artificial intelligence from both technological and human perspectives. PhD students become part of a broader academic community working on related questions and gain access to CHIA s research events, seminars and early-career community. This environment is central to the programme s design. Cambridge emphasizes that students are not expected to conduct their doctoral research in isolation; they will participate in a wider community of researchers addressing overlapping problems in human-inspired AI. What Does “Human-Inspired AI” Mean? The programme s emphasis on human-inspired AI reflects an approach to artificial intelligence that considers both: What AI can learn from humans , and How AI can be developed to work responsibly with and for humans. This can involve questions about areas such as: Human cognition Human communication Human creativity Social interaction Learning Decision-making Human-machine collaboration AI governance Ethics Responsible innovation A project might be technically computational while incorporating insights from psychology or cognitive science. Another could examine interactive AI systems through technical design and human-computer interaction. Other researchers might work on health AI, responsible AI or the governance and societal implications of advanced systems. The programme therefore allows researchers to explore areas in which technical AI intersects with disciplines concerned with human beings, institutions and societies. Research Areas Cambridge specifically identifies several broad areas of research training. Fundamental Human-Level AI This area may involve foundational questions about AI systems and capabilities associated with forms of intelligence found in humans. Research could engage with issues related to: Learning Reasoning Decision-making Generalization Intelligence Human-inspired computational mechanisms Social and Interactive AI AI increasingly interacts directly with individuals and groups. Social and interactive AI can therefore involve research into systems capable of: Communicating with people Understanding social contexts Cooperating with users Supporting decision-making Functioning in interactive environments Such research can also raise questions about trust, communication, social behaviour and responsible system design. Cognitive AI Cognitive AI explores connections between artificial intelligence and human cognition. Researchers may draw on areas such as: Cognitive science Psychology Neuroscience Computer science Machine learning to better understand or reproduce cognitive capabilities computationally. Creative AI Artificial intelligence is increasingly capable of producing: Text Images Music Designs Code Multimedia Creative AI research can therefore involve both technical development and wider questions about human creativity, collaboration, authorship and innovation. Health and Global AI The programme also identifies health and global AI as an important research area. This may provide opportunities to investigate how AI can be designed and deployed across different healthcare and global contexts while paying attention to issues such as: Access Reliability Equity Safety Representation Human needs Institutional differences Responsible AI Responsible AI is another core area. This can encompass questions surrounding: Ethics Governance Accountability Safety Fairness Transparency Human oversight Social consequences Cambridge specifically expects doctoral graduates to develop a critical perspective on governance and ethical challenges arising from human-inspired AI and to understand how those challenges interact with wider society. What the PhD Is Designed to Develop The programme aims to prepare researchers who can contribute critically and constructively to human-inspired AI. According to Cambridge, students should develop the ability to: Work at the frontier of academic research. Understand advanced AI methods and applications. Identify interdisciplinary research problems. Develop technically and methodologically rigorous solutions. Understand ethical and human dimensions of AI. Work on complex problems affecting different sectors of society. The programme therefore emphasizes both specialist expertise and the ability to move between disciplinary perspectives. Who Might Benefit From the Programme? Cambridge identifies several broad groups. The programme may suit students who already want to specialize in human-inspired AI and deepen their: Technical skills Methodological skills Critical research abilities It may also suit researchers whose intellectual “home discipline” is elsewhere but who want to develop an advanced research project incorporating CHIA s interdisciplinary approaches. Finally, the programme is intended to prepare students for careers across: Academia Technology Industry Government Public policy Nonprofit organizations Research institutions Consulting Programme Duration The PhD can be undertaken: Full-time: 3–4 years or: Part-time: 4–7 years. It is classified as a research degree rather than a conventional taught doctoral programme. The full-time course is therefore primarily centred on the student s individual doctoral research project. How the PhD Is Structured Students conduct an individual research project on a topic agreed with CHIA under the guidance of their supervisor. Although research is the programme s core, students also participate in structured professional and intellectual development. PhD researchers are expected to participate in: Weekly student-led seminars or lab meetings CHIA Early Career Community seminars during term Poster presentations at CHIA events At least one oral presentation at a weekly seminar each year Students are additionally encouraged to present their research at: Cambridge events National conferences International conferences Additional Coursework This is an entirely research-based PhD, but students may sometimes undertake additional academic training. With supervisor approval, PhD students may be permitted to attend modules from the MPhil in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence when those modules provide useful technical preparation for the doctoral project. Interdisciplinary researchers may also, where appropriate, audit research-methods classes in other departments. This provides flexibility for candidates whose doctoral research requires skills outside their original academic discipline. Supervision Every PhD student is assigned: A supervisor At least one Academic Advisor Cambridge indicates that supervisor and student are expected to meet individually for approximately 18 hours per year , with additional contact potentially occurring through laboratories, seminars and other research activities. Supervision therefore combines individual guidance with participation in CHIA s wider academic environment. You Must Find a Prospective Supervisor Before Applying This is one of the most important application requirements. Applicants are required to contact a prospective supervisor before submitting the formal PhD application . You should discuss your proposed research with that person and confirm that they are willing and able to accept new PhD students. Applicants need to propose: A research area A topic A potential supervisory relationship At least one named supervisor must come from CHIA s Primary Research Supervisor list . Where appropriate, applicants may also propose co-supervision involving someone from the Potential Co-Supervisor list. However, contacting a supervisor does not guarantee admission, and Cambridge notes that final supervisory arrangements are determined by CHIA. Research Proposal Requirement Applicants must submit a mandatory research proposal. The proposal can be: No more than two A4 pages. Cambridge expects it to outline: Intended research topic Research strategy Understanding of existing work An area where new research is needed Concrete objectives First-year deliverables A credible strategy for achieving those objectives The research proposal may be discussed with the prospective supervisor before the formal application is submitted. Relevant Experience Statement Applicants must also complete a mandatory Relevant Experience section limited to: 2,000 characters. Cambridge specifically asks applicants to explain how their skills and experience have prepared them for the programme s: Computational Mathematical Programming components. This is important because the programme may be interdisciplinary, but it remains a technical AI PhD . Candidates coming from non-computer-science backgrounds should therefore clearly demonstrate sufficient quantitative and technical preparation. Reasons for Applying Applicants also provide a mandatory statement of up to: 1,500 characters explaining their motivation for applying specifically to the PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence. A strong response should therefore explain not simply why the applicant wants a PhD or wants to study AI, but why this particular interdisciplinary Cambridge programme is appropriate for the proposed research. Academic Entry Requirements Cambridge s formal course requirements state that applicants should have achieved: A First-class Honours Degree or international equivalent. A master s-level degree, or equivalent work experience or qualifications, is described as highly desirable . Cambridge accepts applicants from a broad range of academic backgrounds, provided they can demonstrate substantial relevant preparation for the: Computational Mathematical Programming components of their proposed research. Important Note on the Master s Standard The official Cambridge materials contain an additional statement worth noting. The course overview says applicants are normally expected to hold a UK Master s degree with Distinction or an equivalent international qualification . It also says applicants with a Master s awarded at Merit or Pass level may still be considered if they can demonstrate exceptional relevant experience. At the same time, the formal Requirements page states that a First-class Honours undergraduate degree is required and describes a master s-level degree as “highly desirable.” Prospective candidates whose qualifications do not fit the conventional pattern should therefore assess their credentials carefully and, if necessary, contact the course before applying. All applications are ultimately considered on their individual merits. English-Language Requirements Applicants required to demonstrate English-language proficiency face demanding minimum standards. IELTS Academic Required overall score: 7.5 with at least: Listening: 7.0 Writing: 7.0 Reading: 7.0 Speaking: 7.0 TOEFL Internet-Based Test Required overall score: 110 with: Listening: 25 Writing: 25 Reading: 25 Speaking: 25 Cambridge C1 Advanced Applicants need: Grade A or B, overall score 193 , with no element below 185, plus a Language Centre assessment. Cambridge C2 Proficiency Accepted grades are: A, B or C , with at least 200 overall and no element below 185. ATAS Requirement for International Students Cambridge states that applicants who require a visa will need an Academic Technology Approval Scheme (ATAS) certificate if offered admission. Applicants should not apply for ATAS before receiving an offer . The relevant CAH3 code needed for the ATAS application will be included in the offer letter. Application Documents Applicants should prepare the following: Two references Academic transcript Degree certificate where applicable CV or résumé Evidence of English proficiency where required Research proposal of no more than two A4 pages Relevant Experience statement Reasons for Applying statement Cambridge also asks applicants to upload the grading key associated with their transcript if it is not already clearly included. References must be submitted by the deadline. An application is not considered complete until: The application and documents have been submitted Any applicable application fee has been paid The required references have been received Gates Cambridge Applicants Applicants who wish to be considered for a Gates Cambridge Scholarship need additional documentation. This includes: A Gates Cambridge reference A research proposal for PhD applicants The special deadline for applicants in the Gates Cambridge U.S. round is: 14 October 2026. Other applicants seeking Cambridge funding should pay particular attention to the general course funding deadline of: 8 December 2026. Is the Cambridge Human-Inspired AI PhD Fully Funded? Not automatically. This distinction is important. The official Finance page currently states: There are no specific funding opportunities advertised specifically for this course. That does not mean applicants cannot receive funding. Cambridge offers wider university and external funding opportunities, and applicants may potentially be considered for schemes such as Gates Cambridge or other eligible funding sources. However, the PhD itself should not be advertised as automatically fully funded . Prospective students who require financial support should investigate university-wide funding opportunities and submit their course application by the relevant funding deadline. Funding Deadlines For Michaelmas 2027 entry: Course funding deadline: 8 December 2026 Gates Cambridge U.S. round only: 14 October 2026 Applicants seeking funding should not simply rely on the final admission deadline; they should identify the relevant funding competition and make sure all required documents arrive on time. First-Year Progress Review Students are initially admitted to the PhD on a probationary basis . During the first year, they are expected to record: Professional-development activities Seminar participation Training activities Progression to the next year and full PhD registration depends on successful completion of the first-year review. Registration Report As part of the first-year assessment, full-time students submit a written progress report of up to: 8,000 words. The report covers: Research already completed Relevant literature Plans for subsequent years Development of the research project It is then examined orally by two assessors. For part-time students, the equivalent review occurs in their second year. Thesis Requirement In the final year, students submit their doctoral thesis. The thesis should normally not exceed: 60,000 words including: Footnotes Tables Equations but excluding: Appendices Bibliography Photographs Diagrams The thesis is assessed by two examiners, followed by an oral examination covering both the thesis and its wider academic field. Learning Outcomes Graduates are expected to be able to generate and interpret original knowledge that reaches a standard appropriate for peer review and publication. They should also be able to: Design advanced research projects. Modify research in response to unexpected problems. Use cross-disciplinary research methods. Make informed judgments despite incomplete data. Understand governance and ethical questions surrounding AI. Develop substantial knowledge of the history, methods and applications of human-inspired AI. Skills Graduates Will Develop Cambridge expects graduates to leave the programme capable of: Conducting advanced research and development. Developing new techniques and ideas. Communicating with specialist and non-specialist audiences. Working in international and interdisciplinary environments. Taking responsibility for complex projects. Applying research expertise in academic and professional settings. Career Prospects The programme combines advanced technical AI skills with an interdisciplinary understanding of human-centred issues. Cambridge identifies potential career settings including: Technology Health Environment Education Journalism Civil service Consulting Academia Research and development Graduates pursuing academic careers should also be prepared to compete for postdoctoral research positions. Key Dates for 2027 Entry Applications opened: 9 September 2026 Gates Cambridge U.S. funding deadline: 14 October 2026 Application deadline: 8 December 2026 Course funding deadline: 8 December 2026 Course begins: 1 October 2027 Cambridge warns that some courses can close early, so prospective candidates should not assume that waiting until the final deadline is advisable. How to Apply Step 1: Develop a Research Idea Identify a clear research problem relevant to human-inspired AI. The proposal should be technically credible while fitting CHIA s interdisciplinary orientation. Step 2: Identify a Potential Supervisor Review CHIA s list of Primary Research Supervisors. Applicants must contact a prospective supervisor and discuss the project before submitting the formal application. Step 3: Prepare the Two-Page Research Proposal Demonstrate: Knowledge of existing research A genuine research gap Concrete objectives Appropriate methodology First-year deliverables Step 4: Prepare Supporting Materials Gather: Transcripts Degree documentation CV References English-language evidence if necessary Relevant Experience statement Reasons for Applying statement Step 5: Submit Through Cambridge s Applicant Portal Official application page APPLY HERE Step 6: Make Sure References Arrive Your referees must submit their references by the course deadline for the application to be complete. Selection Timeline Applicants who submit by the funding deadline should normally receive a decision by the end of March . Some applicants may be placed on a reserve list, which can delay the process. Cambridge states that decisions should normally be communicated no later than the end of June . Key Information at a Glance Programme: PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence University: University of Cambridge Host: Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence, Institute for Technology and Humanity Country: United Kingdom Degree: Doctor of Philosophy Study mode: Research Full-time duration: 3–4 years Part-time duration: 4–7 years Applications opened: 9 September 2026 Application deadline: 8 December 2026 Course funding deadline: 8 December 2026 Gates Cambridge U.S. deadline: 14 October 2026 Course start: 1 October 2027 Standard academic expectation: First-class Honours degree or international equivalent; master s-level preparation is highly desirable Research proposal: Maximum two A4 pages Supervisor: Applicants must contact a prospective supervisor before applying IELTS requirement where applicable: 7.5 overall, minimum 7.0 in each component TOEFL requirement where applicable: 110 overall, minimum 25 in each component ATAS: Required for relevant visa applicants after an offer Course-specific guaranteed funding: No specific funding opportunity is currently advertised on the course Finance page. Conclusion The University of Cambridge PhD in Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence 2027 offers an unusually interdisciplinary route into advanced artificial intelligence research. Based at the Centre for Human-Inspired Artificial Intelligence within the Institute for Technology and Humanity, the programme is designed for researchers who want to investigate AI not only as a technical system but as a technology deeply connected to human cognition, social interaction, creativity, health, ethics, governance and wider society . Its technical expectations are substantial. Applicants from diverse disciplines are welcome, but they must demonstrate meaningful preparation for the programme s computational, mathematical and programming requirements. For Michaelmas 2027 entry, applications opened on 9 September 2026 , and the principal application and course funding deadline is: 8 December 2026. The programme begins on 1 October 2027 . title: Work//Shift Fellowship 2027: $30,000 Fellowship for Gig Workers, Freelancers and Future-of-Work Leaders
summary: Applications are now open for the Work//Shift Fellowship , a 12-month fellowship created by the Center for Cultural Innovation’s Research to Impact Lab (R2i Lab) for people interested in reimagining the future of work, worker protections, and social safety nets. The fellowship brings together people from different professions, communities, and areas of expertise to examine an increasingly important question: how can systems of economic security, benefits, and worker protections better serve people whose livelihoods fall outside traditional employer-employee arrangements? Freelancers, gig workers, independent contractors, artists, researchers, organizers, policymakers, advocates, entrepreneurs, technologists, community leaders, and others interested in the changing nature of work are among the people the program seeks to engage. Selected fellows will participate in a year-long learning and collaboration experience while receiving a $30,000 stipend for their participation . Applications opened on September 8, 2026 , and the application deadline is October 26, 2026 . Applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, meaning interested candidates are encouraged to apply early rather than waiting until the final deadline. About the Work//Shift Fellowship The Work//Shift Fellowship is built around the changing nature of employment. Many traditional social protection systems were developed around stable employer-employee relationships. However, millions of people earn income through arrangements that do not necessarily fit that model. These include: Freelancers Independent contractors Artists and cultural workers Domestic workers Care workers App-based workers Rideshare and delivery workers Temporary workers Project-based professionals On-demand workers Other people working outside traditional employment structures The Work//Shift Fellowship creates a collaborative environment in which participants can examine these realities and explore new approaches to worker protection and economic security. Instead of beginning with predetermined answers, fellows will engage in inquiry, shared learning, experimentation, imagination, and cross-sector collaboration. The fellowship is particularly interested in creating relationships among people who might not normally work together but who bring different forms of professional knowledge, community experience, lived experience, and expertise to questions about the future of work. Why the Work//Shift Fellowship Was Created The nature of work continues to evolve. Freelance, contract, temporary, platform-based, project-based, and other nontraditional forms of employment have become important parts of modern economies. At the same time, many systems providing benefits and protections remain closely connected to traditional employment arrangements. This creates important questions about how workers outside conventional employment structures can obtain the security and support they need. The Work//Shift Fellowship provides a space for people to examine these challenges collectively. Rather than focusing exclusively on one profession, policy area, or industry, the program deliberately brings together people from multiple disciplines and sectors. The goal is to develop the relationships, knowledge, imagination, and collaborative capacity needed to explore new approaches to worker protections, economic justice, and social safety nets. Who Should Apply for the Work//Shift Fellowship? The program is looking for people who are already thinking seriously about the future of work, particularly freelance, gig, independent, and other forms of nontraditional work. Applicants do not need to have all the answers or arrive with a fully developed project. Potential applicants may include: Organizers and movement builders Policy advocates Researchers Storytellers Cooperative entrepreneurs Systems entrepreneurs Artists Cultural workers Labor advocates Worker advocates Community leaders Academics Technologists Journalists Policymakers Disability rights advocates Domestic workers Home healthcare workers App-based workers Builders working on emerging models of care People developing new ownership models People exploring alternative economic systems Freelancers and independent contractors Applicants can approach the fellowship s central questions from many different professional and community perspectives. What matters is having a meaningful connection to the issues being explored and an interest in contributing to a more equitable future of work. What the Fellowship Is Looking for in Applicants The Work//Shift Fellowship is seeking applicants who demonstrate a genuine commitment to improving conditions for gig workers, freelancers, artists, independent workers, and other workers who may lack traditional employment protections. Successful applicants are expected to demonstrate characteristics including: Commitment to Worker Well-Being Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in improving conditions for freelancers, gig workers, artists, independent contractors, or other workers operating outside conventional employment arrangements. Curiosity The fellowship is designed for people willing to ask difficult questions rather than simply defend existing systems or assumptions. Willingness to Challenge Assumptions Participants should be prepared to reconsider conventional ideas about employment, worker benefits, institutions, economic security, and social safety nets. Openness to New Perspectives Because fellows will come from different sectors and backgrounds, participants should be comfortable learning from perspectives that may differ substantially from their own. Collaborative Mindset The fellowship emphasizes collective learning rather than isolated individual work. Applicants should therefore demonstrate an ability and willingness to collaborate across sectors and disciplines. Community or Professional Relationships Strong candidates are expected to have meaningful relationships within their communities, industries, professions, or fields. Interest in Economic Justice and Worker Protection Applicants should be interested in contributing to a broader ecosystem of people developing new ideas around worker protections and economic justice. Work//Shift Fellowship Learning Journey The 12-month fellowship is structured around four major stages of collective learning. 1. Unlearning The first stage encourages fellows to question existing assumptions about work, institutions, employment structures, and the systems that influence economic life. Participants will examine ideas that may traditionally have been accepted as fixed or inevitable and consider whether different arrangements are possible. 2. Sensemaking Fellows will work toward developing a shared understanding of the political, economic, social, and cultural forces affecting today s workers. This stage is intended to help participants understand the broader environment in which employment systems and worker protections operate. 3. Envisioning Possibilities Participants will examine historical examples, community innovations, emerging models, and other approaches that demonstrate alternative ways of organizing work, support, ownership, care, and economic security. The objective is to expand the range of solutions participants believe may be possible. 4. Building The final stage focuses on turning learning and relationships into new ideas and opportunities for collaboration. Fellows may develop new concepts, partnerships, projects, or other initiatives that contribute to improving the future of work. What Fellows Will Receive One of the most significant features of the Work//Shift Fellowship is its financial support. $30,000 Fellowship Stipend Each fellow will receive a $30,000 stipend for participation in the 12-month fellowship . The stipend supports participation in fellowship activities, including meetings and assigned reading, writing, planning, reflection, and other program-related work. 12-Month Fellowship Experience The fellowship lasts approximately one year, giving participants sufficient time to engage deeply with the program s questions and build meaningful relationships with other fellows. Hybrid Participation The program combines virtual programming with selected in-person gatherings. This structure enables fellows to participate remotely in much of the program while still having opportunities for face-to-face collaboration. Cross-Sector Network Participants will build relationships with people working across different sectors and disciplines. This network is an important part of the fellowship because the program emphasizes relationships and shared learning as major outcomes. Access to Guest Practitioners Fellows will learn from guest practitioners as well as from members of their cohort. Participants will also bring their own professional knowledge, community experience, and expertise into the learning environment. Fellowship Duration and Time Commitment The Work//Shift Fellowship will run for 12 months . Fellows should expect a baseline commitment of approximately 10 hours per month . This time may include: Virtual cohort meetings Reading and learning materials Written assignments Planning activities Individual reflection Discussions with other fellows Collaborative activities Relationship building Fellowship-related preparation The fellowship has intentionally been structured so participants can remain engaged in existing professional or community work. According to the program s FAQ, applicants can participate while working full-time. Cohort Size The Work//Shift Fellowship is expected to select approximately eight fellows . The relatively small cohort is designed to facilitate deeper collaboration, relationship building, discussion, and collective learning among participants. In-Person Convenings Fellows will participate in two in-person cohort convenings during the fellowship. The first gathering is scheduled to take place in Southern California on January 29–30, 2027 . Travel days for the first gathering are scheduled for January 28 and January 31, 2027 . Information about the second in-person convening will be communicated to fellows in advance. Fellowship Start Date The fellowship will begin in January 2027 , starting with an in-person cohort gathering. Selected applicants should therefore consider their availability for the January 2027 launch when applying. Do Applicants Need a Fully Developed Project? No. Applicants do not need to enter the Work//Shift Fellowship with a fully developed project. This is an important feature of the program. The fellowship is designed for people who may already have significant questions, early-stage concepts, lived experience, professional expertise, or emerging ideas but who want an environment where those ideas can evolve through collaboration. The program deliberately creates space for projects and partnerships to emerge through the fellowship experience. Consequently, applicants should not feel that they need to present a complete solution to the challenges facing gig workers or freelancers before applying. Can New Projects Emerge From the Fellowship? Yes. The organizers expect that new ideas, initiatives, collaborations, and potentially projects may emerge as fellows learn and work together. However, producing a particular project is not the sole purpose of the fellowship. The program places significant emphasis on relationships, learning, exploration, and collective imagination. Depending on the ideas that emerge, opportunities to explore additional resources or implementation support may potentially become available. However, fellows should not assume that additional project funding is guaranteed beyond the $30,000 participation stipend. Is Work//Shift Only a Policy Fellowship? No. Policy is one part of the fellowship, but Work//Shift is not exclusively a policy program. Its interdisciplinary approach is one of its distinguishing characteristics. The fellowship welcomes perspectives from people working in areas such as: Public policy Organizing Research Arts and culture Technology Entrepreneurship Worker advocacy Community development Economic development Cooperative models Journalism and storytelling Emerging systems of care and ownership The program s underlying idea is that meaningful approaches to the future of work may emerge when people from different sectors learn together. Do Applicants Need Direct Experience Working With Gig Workers? Not necessarily. Applicants do not have to currently work directly with freelancers or gig workers. However, some present or previous connection to gig work—whether through personal experience, professional work, research, advocacy, policymaking, community engagement, or another indirect connection—may strengthen an application. The key requirement is having a meaningful connection to the issues the fellowship addresses. How the Fellowship Defines Gig Work Work//Shift uses a broad definition of gig work. It generally refers to work occurring outside a traditional, ongoing employer-employee relationship. This can include: Freelance work Contract work Temporary employment Project-based work On-demand work Platform-based work Independent contracting Examples of workers who may fall within this broad category include rideshare drivers, delivery workers, freelancers, artists, cultural workers, caregivers, domestic workers, and other people whose income is derived from short-term or nontraditional working arrangements. Important Work//Shift Fellowship Dates Applicants should carefully note the following timeline: Applications Open: September 8, 2026 First Applicant Webinar: September 17, 2026 Second Applicant Webinar: October 1, 2026 Application Deadline: October 26, 2026 Interviews: November 2–16, 2026 Notification of Decisions: December 7, 2026 Fellowship Begins: January 2027 First In-Person Convening: January 29–30, 2027 Applications are reviewed on a rolling basis , so applicants are encouraged to submit their applications before the final deadline where possible. Work//Shift Fellowship Applicant Webinars Prospective applicants who would like to understand the program in greater detail can participate in virtual information sessions. Two applicant webinars have been scheduled: September 17, 2026 9:00–10:30 AM Pacific Time 11:00 AM–12:30 PM Central Time 12:00–1:30 PM Eastern Time October 1, 2026 5:00–6:30 PM Pacific Time 7:00–8:30 PM Central Time 8:00–9:30 PM Eastern Time Both sessions are intended to cover the same core information, so applicants can attend whichever session works better for their schedule. Participants will be able to learn more about the fellowship, understand the application process, hear what fellows can expect from the program, and ask questions. Application Deadline The deadline to apply for the Work//Shift Fellowship is October 26, 2026 . Because applications are being reviewed on a rolling basis, prospective applicants should consider applying as early as possible. How to Apply for the Work//Shift Fellowship Applications are being accepted online through the Center for Cultural Innovation s application platform. Prospective applicants should first review the complete fellowship information and eligibility expectations before preparing their application. Applicants should pay particular attention to demonstrating their: Connection to gig, freelance, independent, or otherwise unprotected work. Commitment to improving worker conditions. Knowledge or lived experience relevant to the future of work. Curiosity and willingness to challenge conventional assumptions. Ability to collaborate across disciplines and sectors. Existing relationships within relevant communities or professional fields. Interest in contributing to new approaches to worker protections and economic justice. Applicants do not need to submit a fully developed project simply to fit the fellowship s mission. The program explicitly welcomes people whose ideas are still emerging. Click HERE to apply. Why the Work//Shift Fellowship Is Worth Exploring Work//Shift stands out because it approaches the future of work as a collaborative systems challenge rather than focusing narrowly on a single profession or predefined policy solution. The combination of a small cohort, year-long learning experience, interdisciplinary participation, hybrid programming, in-person gatherings, and a substantial $30,000 participation stipend gives selected fellows the opportunity to dedicate meaningful time to exploring complex questions surrounding work and economic security. The fellowship may be particularly relevant to people who believe existing worker protection systems need to evolve alongside changing employment models and who want to explore those questions with others from different professional and community backgrounds. Conclusion The Work//Shift Fellowship 2027 offers gig workers, freelancers, independent contractors, researchers, artists, organizers, advocates, entrepreneurs, policymakers, technologists, and other future-of-work leaders an opportunity to participate in an intensive year-long exploration of worker protections and economic security. Approximately eight fellows will participate in the 12-month hybrid program and receive a $30,000 stipend , while engaging in virtual programming, collaborative learning, relationship building, and two in-person convenings. Importantly, applicants do not need to arrive with a complete project or ready-made solution. Work//Shift is designed to provide the intellectual and collaborative environment in which new relationships, ideas, and initiatives can emerge. Applications are open from September 8 through October 26, 2026 , with applications reviewed on a rolling basis. Application Deadline: October 26, 2026 For complete program information and applications, visit the official Work//Shift Fellowship website. For more global opportunities, click HERE . title: Harvard Kennedy School Master’s Programs 2027–2028: Applications Open for MPP, MPA/ID, MPA and Mid-Career MPA
summary: Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) has opened applications for its 2027–2028 master s degree programs , providing prospective public-service professionals, policy specialists, development practitioners, and experienced leaders with an opportunity to pursue graduate-level education at Harvard University. The programs are designed for people who want to develop the analytical, leadership, policy, management, and quantitative skills needed to address complex public challenges. For the 2027–2028 admissions cycle, prospective students can apply to one of Harvard Kennedy School s master s programs, including the Master in Public Policy (MPP), Master in Public Administration in International Development (MPA/ID), Master in Public Administration (MPA), and Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) . The admission application deadline is December 1, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. (noon) Eastern Time , while the financial aid application deadline is January 15, 2027, at 12:00 p.m. Eastern Time . HKS states that admission and financial-aid decisions are expected in mid-March 2027 . Harvard Kennedy School Master s Admissions 2027–2028 at a Glance Program Length 2026–2027 Tuition Fees Five-Year Average Class Size Master in Public Policy (MPP) 2 years $72,106 258 Master in Public Administration in International Development (MPA/ID) 2 years $74,405 80 Master in Public Administration (MPA) 2 years $72,106 61 Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) 1 year $81,903 256 The tuition figures above are 2026–2027 rates , not guaranteed 2027–2028 tuition. Harvard Kennedy School states that 2027–2028 tuition and fee rates are expected to be published in March 2027 . Important Harvard Kennedy School Application Deadlines Prospective applicants should distinguish between the admission deadline and the financial-aid deadline. Admission Application Deadline December 1, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET All required application materials must be received by this deadline. HKS confirms that the 2027–2028 master s application is currently open. Financial Aid Application Deadline January 15, 2027 at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET Applicants seeking consideration for HKS scholarships and fellowships should complete the financial-aid application by this deadline. Applicants must first submit their admission application before accessing the HKS financial-aid application. Decision Notification Mid-March 2027 HKS states that applicants who are admitted and who submitted a financial-aid application will receive their admission and financial-aid decisions in mid-March 2027. Master in Public Policy (MPP) The Master in Public Policy (MPP) is a two-year program designed for students seeking to understand complex public problems and develop practical solutions. The program combines social-science concepts, analytical methods, policy analysis, and practical experiences. HKS describes the MPP as a rigorous program with a cross-disciplinary core curriculum intended to help students develop the tools necessary to analyze public problems and design solutions. Students can apply their learning through activities including: Case studies Capstone exercises Experiential learning Optional internships Policy analysis Quantitative methods Cross-disciplinary coursework The program is suitable for people interested in areas such as: Public policy Government International affairs Economic policy Social policy Technology policy Climate policy Health policy National security Development Public-sector leadership MPP Eligibility Requirements Applicants to the MPP must have: A bachelor s degree A strong academic record Evidence of quantitative proficiency Undergraduate-level coursework or demonstrated success in areas such as economics, statistics, or calculus A particular undergraduate major is not required. Professional work experience is not mandatory , although HKS notes that it is advantageous and that incoming MPP students typically have approximately 2–3 years of professional work experience . MPP Testing Requirements For the 2027–2028 application cycle, the GRE or GMAT is required unless an applicant qualifies for the applicable waiver. HKS states that the waiver is based on specific quantitative academic coursework and grades. For applicants who did not request a waiver by the relevant deadline, the GRE or GMAT must be submitted. Applicants whose undergraduate degree was not conducted in English may also need to submit an approved English-language proficiency examination, depending on HKS requirements. HKS currently lists TOEFL, IELTS, or Cambridge English examinations for applicants who meet its English-proficiency testing criteria. Master in Public Administration in International Development (MPA/ID) The Master in Public Administration in International Development (MPA/ID) is a two-year program focused on international development, economics, quantitative analysis, policy, and practical development work. It is particularly relevant to people interested in tackling development challenges through government, international organizations, NGOs, development institutions, and other sectors. HKS describes the program as an economics-centered program combining rigorous training in economics and quantitative methods with policy and practical applications. The program can be particularly relevant to applicants interested in: International development Economic development Global development policy Development finance Public-sector reform International organizations Government NGOs Development agencies Economic policy MPA/ID Eligibility Requirements Applicants must have: A bachelor s degree A strong academic record Strong grades in economics and mathematics At least one university-level course in microeconomics At least one university-level course in macroeconomics Calculus through multivariable calculus HKS states that statistics and linear algebra are desirable, although they are not required. Professional experience is not formally required , but it is preferred. HKS notes that most students admitted to the MPA/ID have at least two years of development-related work experience. Applicants who have not completed every prerequisite before submitting the application may be able to complete certain prerequisites before the program begins. MPA/ID Testing Requirements The GRE or GMAT is required. HKS states that applicants are generally most competitive when their quantitative section score is 160 or above on the GRE or 48 or above on the GMAT . These figures should be understood as HKS s stated competitiveness guidance rather than a guarantee of admission. Master in Public Administration (MPA) The Master in Public Administration (MPA) is a two-year program designed for professionals seeking greater responsibility across the public, nonprofit, and private sectors. Unlike the MPP, the two-year MPA has specific professional and graduate-level academic prerequisites. HKS describes the program as flexible, allowing students to build a study plan around their academic interests and professional goals. Students can also pursue concurrent degrees in areas such as business, law, medicine, and other professional disciplines. MPA Eligibility Requirements Applicants must have: A bachelor s degree A strong academic record At least three years of professional work experience by September 1 of the year they enroll At least four qualifying graduate-level courses similar to courses in the MPP core curriculum At least two quantitative graduate-level courses among those qualifying courses Qualifying graduate-level coursework can include subjects such as: Economics Financial management International business International development Management Mathematics Quantitative analysis Statistics Politics and advocacy Other related fields A relevant graduate degree can also satisfy the graduate-level coursework requirement in appropriate circumstances. This makes the two-year MPA particularly different from the MPP and MPA/ID: having a bachelor s degree alone is not sufficient for the MPA. Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) The Mid-Career Master in Public Administration (MC/MPA) is a one-year program intended for experienced professionals who want to strengthen their leadership capabilities, develop specialized expertise, and prepare for greater impact in public service or other sectors. HKS describes the program as an intensive one-year program that gives experienced professionals flexibility to design a study plan around their interests and career objectives. MC/MPA Eligibility Requirements Applicants must have: A bachelor s degree A strong academic record At least seven years of professional work experience by June 30 of the year they plan to enroll The program is therefore aimed at a substantially more experienced applicant population than the MPP or MPA/ID. HKS notes that competitive MC/MPA applicants typically have considerably more professional experience than the seven-year minimum. What Is the Application Process? Harvard Kennedy School requires applicants to submit an online application together with supporting materials. A complete master s application generally includes: Online application Essays Résumé or CV Three letters of recommendation Academic transcripts Required standardized test scores English-language proficiency documentation where applicable $100 application fee or an applicable fee waiver Requirements vary depending on the program. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the requirements for one HKS master s program automatically apply to all four programs. GRE and GMAT Requirements Standardized-test requirements differ by degree. MPP GRE or GMAT is required unless the applicant qualifies for the applicable waiver. MPA/ID GRE or GMAT is required. MPA GRE or GMAT is required unless the applicant qualifies for the applicable waiver. MC/MPA GRE and GMAT are not required . Applicants may voluntarily submit scores for consideration. For the 2027–2028 admission cycle, HKS states that the GRE/GMAT waiver deadline has already passed. Applicants applying to the MPP or MPA who did not previously obtain a waiver therefore need to submit the relevant test results. English-Language Proficiency English-language proficiency requirements depend on an applicant s educational background. For the MPP, HKS states that non-native English speakers who did not earn an undergraduate degree conducted in English must submit results from an approved English-language examination such as: TOEFL IELTS Cambridge English For the 2027–2028 cycle, HKS also introduced a new TOEFL scoring model. Applicants who took the TOEFL after January 2026 need an overall score of 5 or better , with the most competitive applicants also having at least 5 in each section. Applicants who took the TOEFL before January 2026 need an overall score of 100 or better , with the most competitive applicants having at least 25 in each section. Applicants should check the official HKS requirements for their specific program before registering for an examination. Financial Aid, Scholarships and Fellowships Although the master s admissions opportunity is not itself a scholarship, Harvard Kennedy School provides financial assistance opportunities for admitted students. HKS states that scholarships and fellowships are available to both U.S. and international students . Financial support can include: HKS scholarships HKS fellowships Research-center fellowships Harvard Committee on General Scholarships funding Other Harvard-wide funding opportunities Many HKS scholarships and fellowships are awarded primarily based on merit. HKS states that its assessment of merit can consider: Academic achievement Intellectual distinction Leadership capabilities Quantitative proficiency Commitment to public service Diverse experiences and backgrounds Financial need can also be considered when determining award amounts. Learn More HERE Financial Aid Deadline Applicants seeking HKS financial assistance should submit the financial-aid application by: January 15, 2027 at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET HKS emphasizes that there are very few opportunities to apply for fellowship or scholarship funding after admission or enrollment, making it important for applicants who want funding to complete the process on time. International Students and Applicants From Africa Harvard Kennedy School s master s programs are open to international applicants. HKS explicitly states that its scholarships and fellowships are available to both U.S. and international students. It also states that institutional funding does not discriminate against applicants or students on the basis of citizenship, race, ethnicity, sex, or other protected classifications. This means applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania, and other parts of the world can apply if they meet the relevant program requirements. For applicants from Ghana and other countries where English may be the language of university instruction, it is particularly important to check HKS s English-language testing rules based on the language in which the undergraduate degree was conducted. International applicants should also investigate the U.S. student-visa process and any financial documentation required after admission. Can Recent Graduates Apply? Yes, depending on the program. The MPP and MPA/ID do not require professional work experience, although HKS says professional experience is advantageous and common among admitted students. The MPA , however, requires three years of professional work experience plus qualifying graduate-level preparation. The MC/MPA requires at least seven years of professional work experience. Therefore, someone who has recently completed a bachelor s degree and has limited professional experience should pay particular attention to the MPP and MPA/ID requirements rather than assuming that all HKS master s programs have identical eligibility criteria. Important Application Rule: One Master s Program HKS states that applicants may apply to only one master s degree program per admissions cycle . This means applicants should carefully research the differences between the MPP, MPA/ID, MPA, and MC/MPA before submitting their application. The choice should be based on the applicant s: Academic background Quantitative preparation Professional experience Career objectives Interest in public policy or administration Development experience Leadership experience Eligibility for the specific program What Does Harvard Kennedy School Look For? HKS receives more qualified applicants than it can admit, and its admissions committee reviews the complete application when making admissions decisions. Applicants should therefore present a coherent profile showing how their academic background, professional experience, leadership, public-service interests, and future goals connect to the program they are applying for. Important areas include: Academic Preparation Strong academic performance is important across the master s programs. Depending on the program, quantitative preparation can be particularly important. Professional Experience Work experience requirements vary significantly. MPP: not required MPA/ID: not required but preferred MPA: at least 3 years MC/MPA: at least 7 years Leadership Applicants should be able to demonstrate leadership potential and meaningful contributions through their academic, professional, community, or other experiences. Public-Service Commitment HKS is specifically focused on preparing people to address public challenges and make an impact across government, nonprofit, international, and other sectors. Quantitative Ability Quantitative preparation is particularly relevant to the MPP and MPA/ID and is also part of the MPA requirements. HKS states that each master s program includes a quantitative component. Application Materials to Prepare Applicants should begin preparing their materials well before the December deadline. A useful preparation checklist includes: Academic transcripts Updated résumé/CV Three recommendation letters Required essays GRE/GMAT results where required English-language test results where required Application fee or waiver documentation Financial-aid materials, if seeking HKS funding HKS recommends that applicants complete required examinations sufficiently early to allow scores to be received by the application deadline. AI Use in the 2027–2028 Application HKS has introduced an optional AI disclosure question for the 2027–2028 application cycle. The school states that applicants may disclose their use of generative AI in the application in 250 words or fewer . The disclosure is for data-collection purposes and is not shared with the Admissions Committee or used in the admissions decision. At the same time, HKS states that generative AI or machine-learning software may be used only to assist with editing or identifying grammatical errors in application essays. The substantive content of the essays must be the applicant s own work. Applicants should therefore carefully follow HKS s current AI-use instructions rather than using AI to generate their substantive application responses. Why the Programs Are Relevant to Public-Service Careers Harvard Kennedy School s master s programs cover different aspects of public leadership and policy. Depending on the degree, students can develop skills related to: Policy analysis Economics Quantitative methods International development Public administration Management Leadership Governance Public-sector decision-making International affairs Social policy Economic policy Development practice The MPP, for example, emphasizes analytical methods and practical policy problem-solving, while the MPA/ID focuses heavily on economics and quantitative methods for international development. The MPA provides greater flexibility for experienced professionals, while the MC/MPA is structured for established mid-career professionals. Choosing Between the Four Programs Applicants should carefully distinguish the programs before applying. Consider the MPP if you: Have a bachelor s degree Want rigorous public-policy training Have quantitative preparation Are interested in solving complex public problems Do not yet have extensive professional experience Consider the MPA/ID if you: Have strong economics and mathematics preparation Are interested in international development Have completed microeconomics, macroeconomics, and calculus Want economics-centered development training Are interested in international organizations, government, development institutions, or NGOs Consider the MPA if you: Have at least three years of professional experience Have substantial graduate-level coursework or a qualifying graduate degree Want a flexible public-administration curriculum Are preparing for greater responsibility across sectors Consider the MC/MPA if you: Have at least seven years of professional experience Are an established professional Want an intensive one-year program Are seeking additional leadership and policy capabilities These distinctions are based on HKS s current program requirements and descriptions. Key Dates to Remember September 2026: 2027–2028 master s application cycle opens. December 1, 2026, 12:00 p.m. ET: Master s admission application deadline. January 15, 2027, 12:00 p.m. ET: Financial-aid application deadline. Mid-March 2027: Admission and financial-aid decisions announced. April 2027: Admitted students must respond to their offers by the stated response deadline. How to Apply Interested applicants should begin by reviewing the official Harvard Kennedy School master s admissions information and identifying the one program that best matches their academic and professional background. Official HKS Master s Admissions: HERE Online Application: HERE Applicants should review the official requirements carefully because standardized testing, academic prerequisites, professional-experience requirements, and English-language requirements vary between programs. Conclusion The Harvard Kennedy School Master s Programs 2027–2028 admissions cycle provides prospective students with the opportunity to pursue graduate education in public policy, international development, public administration, and mid-career public leadership. The four principal master s pathways differ considerably in their intended student profiles and prerequisites. The MPP is a two-year policy program that does not require professional experience, while the MPA/ID provides rigorous economics and quantitative training for international development. The two-year MPA is intended for professionals with at least three years of work experience and substantial graduate-level preparation, while the one-year MC/MPA requires at least seven years of professional experience. International applicants are eligible to apply, and HKS provides scholarship and fellowship opportunities for both U.S. and international students. However, financial assistance is a separate process from admission, and applicants seeking funding should submit their financial-aid application by January 15, 2027 . The most important deadline for prospective students is December 1, 2026 at 12:00 p.m. (noon) ET , when the master s admission application and required materials must be received. Because applicants can apply to only one HKS master s program per admissions cycle , prospective students should carefully compare the programs, verify their eligibility, prepare the required tests and documents, and build an application that clearly demonstrates their academic preparation, professional experience, leadership potential, and commitment to public service. title: ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027: Paid Public Health Traineeships in Stockholm, Sweden
summary: The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) Traineeship Programme 2027 offers recent university graduates an opportunity to gain practical professional experience within a European Union agency working to prevent and control infectious diseases. The programme is designed for graduates who are beginning their professional careers and want to develop practical knowledge, understand the work of an EU public health institution, and apply the knowledge gained through their university studies in a professional environment. For the 2027 cohort, ECDC is offering 12 traineeship positions across different professional areas and functions of the Centre. The traineeships will last between five and nine months , depending on the placement and applicable arrangements. The programme is based at ECDC in Stockholm, Sweden , and provides selected trainees with a monthly traineeship grant and a travel allowance. The programme is particularly relevant to graduates interested in public health, epidemiology, infectious diseases, data and digital solutions, science communication, social and behavioural sciences, administration, and related fields. About the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control , commonly known as ECDC, is an agency of the European Union that works to strengthen Europe’s defences against infectious diseases. ECDC supports European countries and public health institutions by: Monitoring infectious disease developments. Collecting and analysing public health information. Identifying emerging and cross-border health threats. Assessing risks associated with communicable diseases. Supporting outbreak preparedness and response. Providing scientific and technical advice. Strengthening disease surveillance. Promoting public health cooperation. Supporting training and professional development. Communicating reliable information about infectious disease risks. Through its traineeship programme, ECDC gives recent graduates the opportunity to gain first-hand knowledge of how a European public health agency operates and how scientific, technical, administrative, and communication functions contribute to public health protection. What Is the ECDC Traineeship Programme? The ECDC Traineeship Programme is a professional development opportunity aimed at recent university graduates who are entering the early stages of their careers. The programme is intended to help trainees: Gain a practical understanding of ECDC and its role within the European Union. Learn about the Centre’s work in identifying, assessing, and communicating current and emerging threats to human health. Acquire practical knowledge of the day-to-day work of ECDC units. Apply academic knowledge and technical skills in a professional setting. Develop professional competencies and workplace experience. Improve their understanding of European public health procedures and institutional cooperation. Build a foundation for future professional opportunities in public health, science, policy, administration, communications, and related areas. Trainees work within a specific ECDC unit or function and are expected to contribute to activities relevant to their educational background and placement. ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027: Key Details Programme: ECDC Traineeship Programme 2027 Host organisation: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control Opportunity type: Paid, non-statutory traineeship Number of positions: 12 Duration: Five to nine months Location: Stockholm, Sweden Application period: 8 September to 5 October 2026 Application deadline: 5 October 2026 at 12:00 noon, Stockholm time Expected interview period: Mid-October to mid-December 2026 Expected start period: The source provides a general traineeship FAQ indicating a February to April start period; applicants should follow the dates communicated for the 2027 cohort. Application platform: ECDC e-recruitment portal Available Traineeship Areas The ECDC recruitment portal lists traineeship positions across a range of professional and scientific areas. The available positions include opportunities related to infectious diseases, public health, digital services, social sciences, communication, and organisational support. Examples of listed traineeship areas include: 1. Respiratory Viruses This area may be relevant to graduates interested in respiratory infectious diseases, disease surveillance, epidemiology, laboratory science, public health research, and the monitoring of respiratory virus threats. Potential activities may involve supporting work related to: Respiratory virus surveillance. Epidemiological information. Disease monitoring. Public health preparedness. Scientific analysis. Risk assessment and communication. The exact responsibilities depend on the individual vacancy description. 2. Digital Solutions The Digital Solutions traineeship may be relevant to graduates with backgrounds in: Information technology. Computer science. Data management. Digital systems. Information systems. Software or technology-related fields. Digital transformation and service delivery. Potential activities may involve supporting digital tools, information systems, data-related work, technology services, or other digital functions within ECDC. 3. Antimicrobial Resistance and Healthcare-Associated Infections This traineeship area may interest graduates working in or studying: Public health. Epidemiology. Microbiology. Infectious diseases. Antimicrobial resistance. Healthcare-associated infections. Health policy. Infection prevention and control. The work may contribute to ECDC activities concerning antimicrobial resistance, healthcare-associated infections, surveillance, prevention, and public health guidance. 4. Food-, Water-, Vector-Borne and Zoonotic Diseases This area may be suitable for graduates interested in infectious diseases transmitted through: Food. Water. Vectors such as mosquitoes and ticks. Animals. Environmental exposure. Relevant academic backgrounds may include public health, epidemiology, microbiology, environmental health, veterinary public health, infectious disease research, and related disciplines. 5. Social and Behavioural Sciences This traineeship may be relevant to graduates with backgrounds in: Psychology. Sociology. Behavioural sciences. Social sciences. Public health. Health communication. Behaviour change. Risk perception. Community engagement. Potential work may involve understanding public attitudes, behaviours, communication needs, and social factors that influence infectious disease prevention and public health responses. 6. Trainees are responsible for determining whether they must pay income tax. Tax obligations depend on the trainee’s individual circumstances and the applicable national rules. Applicants should seek appropriate tax advice where necessary. The monthly grant should therefore not automatically be treated as a conventional salary.
